subject: Animation
title: The Ink and Paint Department
description: A 60-second lesson on The Ink and Paint Department.

hook.text: Behind every Disney classic was a department of mostly women who hand-colored every frame.

buildup.text: The Ink and Paint workers traced animator drawings onto clear cels and painted them by hand.

discovery.text: At its peak, hundreds of women worked in the department, producing thousands of painted cels daily.

twist.text: Despite their essential role, Ink and Paint workers were paid less than male animators.

climax.text: When xerography replaced hand-inking in the 1960s, the department slowly disappeared.

punchline.text: Women painted every frame Disney ever dreamed.

quiz.question: What was the Ink and Paint department's primary role?
options: Writing the stories for Disney films
Hand-coloring animation cels by tracing and painting each frame
Designing the characters for each film

details.summary: Disney's Ink and Paint department was staffed almost entirely by women who meticulously traced and colored every frame of Disney's classic films. Their invisible labor was essential to Disney's output, yet they received almost no recognition for decades.
details.whyItMatters: The Ink and Paint department reveals animation history's gender dynamics. Hundreds of women did essential production work while male animators received creative credit and higher status, a pattern that persisted throughout the industry.
takeaways: The Ink and Paint department was staffed almost entirely by women
These workers traced and colored every frame of Disney's classic films
Their essential labor went largely unrecognized for decades

faq.question: What did the Ink and Paint department do?
faq.answer: Women in the department hand-traced animator drawings onto celluloid sheets in ink, then painted each cel by hand with precise color mixtures. Every frame of every classic Disney film passed through their hands. It was meticulous, essential, and grueling work.

faq.question: Why were the Ink and Paint workers mostly women?
faq.answer: Disney deliberately hired women for these roles, considering the detail work suited to female workers while reserving creative animation positions for men. This segregation reflected broader gender norms but also meant women's contributions to Disney's masterpieces went uncredited.
